#7910. Rachael Leigh Cook Talks Her New Hallmark Rom-Com, Parenting Teens & 'She's All That'

The Double Booked for the Holidays star (and mom of two) opens up about being in the parenting-a-teen trenches with the rest of us.

For a whole generation of us, Rachael Leigh Cook will forever be Laney Boggs walking down those stairs in *the* red dress. But these days, in addition to being a busy working actor, she’s also a mom of a 13-year-old and an 11-year-old, which means she’s living through the tween and teen years like the rest of us. (“Mixed job performance reviews from my 13-year-old, for sure,” she admits.) And, yep, her daughter has even seen Cook’s iconic ‘90s movies like She’s All That. Her review? She’s glad her mom’s eyebrows grew back.

Also like so many of us, Cook’s a total sucker for a cozy holiday rom-com. It just so happens she’s currently starring in one: Double Booked for the Holidays, now streaming on Hallmark+. She plays identical twins Abigail and Charlie, who head to Wales to a bookish Airbnb for their first Christmas after losing their mom.

When we caught up with Cook, she filled us in on playing double duty, the “say yes” theory that led her to her boyfriend, and the ‘90s icons she considers go-to comfort watches.

Scary Mommy: You're playing twins, which means you're your own scene partner. Which sister is more you, Abigail or Charlie?

Rachael Leigh Cook: I think our producers thought of Abigail as the sort of anchor character in the story. Her love story gets a little bit more screen time, but I just related a lot more to the Charlie character. So that sort of just felt a little easier to latch onto and to have fun with because I'm always just trying to have the best time. When you make these movies, I feel like the audience's enjoyment is my responsibility. If the scene is informational, I'm going to try to make it go fast for you. If it could be a little bit silly, I'm going to make it as silly as they let me. I want it to be fun for you. So when I got to be Charlie and I felt like I got to deliver a little bit more razzle dazzle or whatever you want to call it, that's what felt the best.

SM: What did you do to make the twins feel different? Because I literally had to keep reminding myself there are not, in fact, two of you.

RLC: Julie, that's the nicest thing that you could say. That's what I was utterly terrified of. I read the script, and I thought, Uh-oh, this is going to just seem like I'm talking to myself if I'm not careful because I'm very guilty of being a multi-screen viewer. I'm not afraid to look at my phone. Those shows where if someone just looks at someone and it means something and then you don't understand the next scene, I'm lost. I can't handle it. So I knew that for people like me who might also drift off and just get a snack, I needed everything to be clear. I couldn't have people dipping in and out and feeling confused. This is a holiday movie. We're not trying to confuse anyone.

I really just tried to separate vocally and work from the top of my vocal range to the basement. And that's a little bit difficult because I realized that at the top I can't project very well. But other than that, I feel like it worked pretty well. I just tried to separate the physicality as much as I could so that people weren't confused. We realized that just because of the quick schedule we're on, I couldn't even change hair between the two very much. I got concerned pretty early on that it was just going to be a giant melting pot of too much of me, and that seemed just real bad. So I thought I got to just separate them as much as I can. And if I'm bad, I'm bad, but no one's confused.

SM: You once said something I loved, which is that you’re happiest to be alive when you're living wholly unique experiences.

SM: Did Christmas in a Welsh bookshop movie count?

RLC: Absolutely. I didn't even read the whole script before I said yes. I probably shouldn't admit that, but I just thought no one's going to call and ask if I want to play my own twin ever again in Wales. I can figure out the rest. I'll be fine. This is a say yes moment if there ever was one.

SM: For sure. Any other recent examples that made that list?

RLC: It was I think a little over a year and a half ago, but I remember this day because I got two back-to-back emails. And, listen, most days as an actor are things like, Yeah, they don't want you for that part or Oh, here's a two-cent residual check or whatever. It ain't all glamor.

But one day I got two back-to-back emails and one of them said, "Do you want to be a guest on Name That Tune?" And the other one right after it said, "Do you want to be in a float in the Hollywood Christmas Parade?" And I just wrote, "Yes, send, yes, send." And before I knew it, I had two completely wild experiences because of those things. Because of one of them, I met my now boyfriend, and because of the other one, I got to go and play Name That Tune with Michelle Williams from Destiny's Child.

So that was a pretty awesome validation of my say yes theory.

SM: I am obsessed with everything you just said. Also, that sounds like its own little mini Hallmark movie — you met your boyfriend?! Come on.

RLC: I mean, Hallmark can do just about no wrong as far as I'm concerned. They provide so much cortisol-free entertainment for people with wildly stressful jobs and lives, and I'm all about it. I'm drinking that Kool-Aid all day.

SM: Me too, sister. Well, I want to dip into some nostalgia because we actually recently put your She's All That dress on our list of pop culture dresses we were all obsessed with growing up. You’ve said it didn’t really change you, but rather it revealed your confidence. Do you have a real-life article of clothing that does that for you now?

RLC: I almost don't want to draw attention to it because I know that you'll then see how many times I've worn this. I have this great tracksuit by... Oh my gosh, I can't remember. Why can't I even remember who makes it? I got it in New York. It's sort of cranberry colored. It has stripes on the sleeves. I can get this information to you. And it's matching pants and a top, and there's almost nowhere that this set can't go because you can wear it with heels and some big jewelry and it feels very sort of casual, upscale, athleisure, or you can wear it with sneakers and no extra anything and it just looks like you put some thought into it.

That is my I don't know what to wear outfit. Everyone should have one of those.

SM: Oh, 100%. Well, I know you're in the thick of the tween and early teen years. I have a 13-year-old and a 15-year-old, so we're in it. Number one: how are you?

RLC: Thank you for asking. I think I'm doing fine, but yeah, mixed job performance reviews from my 13-year-old, for sure. I sometimes just feel like I can do no right, and it's really difficult. I'm trying to take what my friends with older kids say about, Oh, it's just because they feel so safe with you that they can just live as their frustrated self, and then they go to school and they behave well and toe the line and all of that. So I'm just like, yep, I'm so honored, so honored. It's a bumpy ride over here, but it's also the very best, and I wouldn't change a thing about it.

I'm absolutely horrified because I can see almost the first break of dawn's light far in the distance of them wanting to leave my home, and that is totally unacceptable. I'm like, "No, you have to stay my babies forever." My son is 11 and still doesn't love sleeping with all the lights off, so I'm hopeful that I can feel like I'm still the mom to a young child in some small ways anyway.

SM: Like you said, it's very day-to-day, so we're just rolling with it. But it's also cool to get to see more of who they're becoming, which I think is really fun.

RLC: Very well said. That's the incredible part. Even though it's the worst thing ever when those memory photos show up on your phone of them as a baby — it's painful because you can't have that time anymore — it's like, "Well, yeah, but I also didn't know you as well."

SM: Exactly. Your daughter, Charlotte, is 13 now… has she watched She’s All That or Josie and the Pussycats yet?

RLC: She has. And they came with me to a screening of Josie at the Hollywood Forever Cemetery pretty recently, and there were, I think, 4,000 people there. It was a big group, and I feel really grateful to them and the revival houses because I don't know if in this day and age there's any chance that my kids would be able to experience work I've done on that scale ever again. I think the kids were mostly in it for the candy, but they were very respectful.

I think my daughter said she's glad my eyebrows grew back, and so am I.

SM: Kids… they sure know how to keep you humble! Last question: As a ‘90s and early ‘00s icon, you’re a comfort watch for a lot of us.

SM: I’m curious, what is your comfort watch?

RLC: Oh, man. I geeked out over... I met Elizabeth Shue one time. I can't tell you how many times I've seen Adventures in Babysitting. So someone like that. I've never met Molly Ringwald, but I would be the least cool human in the world. I grew up on John Hughes movies and her. So yeah, I'd say those.

SM: I love it. You’ve been a true joy, and it's such an honor to meet you.

RLC: Mine! And you're doing great. You really are.

SM: You too. We’ll get to the other side of all this; we will.

SM: Oh, babe, that’s a convo for a whole other interview.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

#7909. Jennifer Garner reveals how Once Upon a Farm became a $724 million company without sacrificing its values at Motherly’s State of Motherhood event

Home / Health & Wellness / Women's Health

Motherly hosted some of the country’s most influential women leaders for a State of Motherhood event that took a deep look at what the last decade reveals about moms, and what we need going forward.

By Audrey Goodson Kingo Updated Nov. 19, 2026

Moms may be burned out and lonely right now – but we don’t have to accept it.

That was the theme of Motherly’s State of Motherhood event on Monday, which brought together some of the most powerful women in business, media and advocacy to diagnose how moms have fared during the last tumultuous decade, and detail what we need going forward.

The conversation was driven by an in-depth analysis of Motherly’s own research. Every year since 2018, we’ve polled thousands of moms (more than 60,000 in fact!) for our annual State of Motherhood survey. And every year, moms have told us they’re scaling back at work and having fewer children than they’d prefer, but they’re still feeling isolated and overwhelmed. In 2025, 70% of moms said motherhood is lonelier than expected and in 2026, 42% felt more burned out than in the previous year.

“The truth is that our expectations of what it means to be a good mom changed faster than the systems built around to support her, and Gen Z moms are running into that gap even earlier,” said Motherly’s CEO Sharon Yi in her opening remarks. “But none of us should have to sacrifice our sanity, our careers, our identities to have children, and no mother should have to carry it alone.”

Leaders from organizations at the Clinton Foundation, the Andrew Carnegie Foundation, the ACLU, and the Vote Mama Foundation, joined together with executives at JP Morgan, Pfizer, Coterie, IKEA, and Paramount, to hear from women who are working tirelessly to create a world where moms feel supported, connected, and respected.

That included actress Jennifer Garner, who talked about her work as an ambassador for Save the Children and as co-founder of organic children’s nutrition company Once Upon a Farm.

Garner kicked off the event in a fireside chat that touched on everything from finding community as a mom to the importance of advocating for children and families.

“Every kid deserves healthy, real food, an education, and parents who have a roof over their heads, food in their bellies, and time and space and energy and support to love their kids,” she said. Traveling around the country for her work with Save the Children, she described seeing families stretch food-bank, WIC, and SNAP resources to feed their children.

That’s why Once Upon a Farm worked hard to become the first WIC-certified company offering organic refrigerated baby food, she said. The company is now WIC-certified in 22 states. For Garner, it’s about dignity and choice: families using public benefits should be able to access high-quality food.

It’s all baked in, pun intended, to the company’s social mission to “drive systemic change in childhood nutrition for a happier, healthier, more equitable world,” Garner says. In 2021, the company transitioned its corporate structure from an LLC to a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC), which legally requires it to balance profitability with its social and environmental impact. It’s a challenging path for a business to pursue, which is why there are fewer than 20 publicly-traded PBCs, and Once Upon a Farm is the only one focused on kids. Towards those goals, Garner said, the company has donated a million meals to kids in rural America, and it pays a premium for produce “so that the people who are growing and picking our food are recruited ethically, and have a say in their safety and what their workday looks like.”

When it comes to balancing the demands of her multi-hyphenite life with motherhood, Garner didn’t hold back. On her non-negotiables, she joked, “I work out every day… unless I don’t. I read every night until I fall asleep… one page or none. I go to church… when I can. My kids come first… except for weeks where it’s crazy and I tell them they come first from afar.”

Finding the right balance changes day by day, Garner said. She assesses who needs her most in a given moment, including herself. “You get to choose moment to moment what you do and what your family needs,” she said to the moms in the room.

She also encouraged moms to come together to help defeat the loneliness that Motherly’s data revealed. “We’re literally meant to be in community,” she described. “When my second was born, I joined a baby group for second-time moms, and that is the most active group chat on my phone to this day.”

Plus, she added, small groups of committed moms have the power to make real change.

“We all love our babies the same. And when you realize that, that every mother in the world loves their baby the way you love yours, which seems impossible, but it is true, that also connects you to every other mother,” she said. “And then you feel like, how can I help every other mother who doesn’t have the advantages I have?”

Next up was a panel about the state of motherhood in 2026, breaking down Motherly’s data showing that moms are increasingly burned out, and figuring out fixes to help. Featuring some of the most influential women working to make the United States a better place for families, the panelists pointed out that burnout is a structural problem — not an individual failure — and that collective action can turn broad public support for family policies into change.

“I think motherhood in America is impossible by design,” said Reshma Saujani, the founder and CEO of Moms First, a national non-profit organization working to advance paid leave and affordable childcare for working families. “Why does the school day end at 2:30 and the workday end at six? Why do we pay more for our childcare than our mortgage? Why do one out of four women go back to work two weeks after having a baby?”

Lauren Smith Brody, the founder of The Fifth Trimester and co-founder of Chamber of Mothers, said she’s optimistic that federal lawmakers will soon advance legislation to help moms across the country, including paid family leave, affordable childcare for all, and measures to improve maternal health outcomes. “I feel a lot of hope as we walk into these offices on Capitol Hill and we make a lot of behind the scenes connections between Democratic offices and Republican offices, because guess what? They actually do want many of the same things,” she said. “Moms are top of the list. They know that our voting power is unmatched. They know that they need us. They know that we voted them in and can vote them out.”

“I am telling you standing right here, [affordable] childcare and paid leave will get passed in 2029 within the first hundred days,” Saujani said. “I don’t care who is elected president because we are getting this done.”

It’s all about moms coming together to hold leaders accountable, said Ailen Arreaza, the executive director of the national nonprofit parents organization ParentsTogether. “Moms often feel it’s our sole responsibility to protect our kids, and feel shame when we think we’ve failed — especially when it comes to technology,” she said. “One of the best ways that we can hold companies accountable is by sharing our stories. We do a lot of work with parents who have lost children to big tech, and their stories are so powerful,” she said. “That also helps with the shame. When we talk to each other about what we are struggling with, what we are facing, that shame evaporates.”

Michelle Jawando, the CEO of Omidyar Network, a philanthropy organization working to foster responsible technology and AI development, said she’s encouraged by the fact that the mistakes of the “move-fast-and-break-things” era in Silicon Valley are providing a roadmap for more responsible tech development going forward. “I believe that everything that happened in that proceeding era gives us an opportunity to get AI right,” she said, pointing to California, which recently passed the strongest AI companion chatbot legislation in the country.

The morning’s final panel, moderated by the host of Motherly’s new podcast, Daniela Gysler-Wood, provided practical ways mothers can protect their physical and mental well-being.

Dr. Bayo Curry-Winchell, a board certified family medicine physician and the author of the upcoming book How to Talk to Your Doctor, encouraged moms to keep seeking answers if they’re feeling unwell. Her advice? If a clinician says you are fine but you do not feel fine, say, “I understand that you think I’m fine, but I’m not. What are the next steps?”

She also suggested asking, “What three to five possibilities are on your working list?” This helps you understand the range of possibilities if your doctor is focused on just one diagnosis.

When it comes to getting enough rest, celebrate the small wins, said Megan Holm, the women’s sleep research lead at sleep technology company Eight Sleep. “Sleep when you can, and you don’t need to check off everything on your to-do list in order to put your head on the pillow. You can take a 30-minute nap,” she said.

“I think we’ve all just accepted that exhaustion is part of motherhood, and I don’t think that’s where we should be,” said Victoria Thain Gioia, the co-founder and CEO of Perelel, an OB/GYN-founded and doctor-formulated vitamin and supplement brand. “To get through the day and stay sane, and to take care of small children, and do your job, you need to be nutritionally sufficient, not depleted. So while it can sometimes be overhyped, the conversation about protein, collagen, lactoferrin and nutrients that can actually support your energy [is important]. We really need to focus on care for mom beyond just pregnancy and postpartum.”

When it comes to protecting our mental well-being, the panelists encouraged moms to let go of guilt and connect with other parents. “Check in on your friends, nurture your friendships, don’t ask everything of your partner or your spouse, and ask for help,” said Elise Hu, the host of TED Talks Daily, a flagship podcast from TED Conferences. “Asking for help doesn’t just benefit you, the person who needs the help, it also benefits the helper because think about all the times that you have been asked for advice or counsel. That’s such a tribute to you, right? Because somebody is saying to you, ‘I trust you and I trust your advice and I trust your counsel.’ It nurtures the connection on both ends, not only for the helpee, but also the helper.”

The moms in the room didn’t just leave with actionable advice and encouragement – although there was plenty on tap – they also took home a Happ Paige Mini full of goodies, including Once Upon a Farm snacks, Perelel Collagen+ Defense Supplements, Shiseido Sun Protector Clear Stick Sunscreen, Then I Met You Cleansing Balm, Ursa Major Golden Hour Recovery Cream, Merit Shade Slick, and the new Bentgo Lift Chug Lid water bottle.

Guests also got a chance to try out a mini version of Eight Sleep’s pod, an intelligent mattress cover that uses built-in biometric sensors to track your sleep and automatically adjust its temperature. “In May, we released pregnancy mode, which is automatic temperature support to support women as they go through pregnancy and up to 24 weeks postpartum,” said Holm, Eight Sleep’s women’s research lead, during the second panel. “As you grow a child, the environment around you feels really hot and uncomfortable. So we automatically make sure that when you can rest, and even if it’s not for eight hours every night, you’re comfortable.”

And bestselling author Loryn Brantz greeted guests as they walked into the room, signing free copies of her new release, I Am a Spicy Nugget, as well as copies of her New York Times bestseller, Poems of Parenting. Some lucky guests also received a signed print.

Motherly’s CEO Sharon Yi closed out the day with a call to action for all of the “incredible, powerful, influential” women in the room: “From all these conversations, I heard over and over that we need community, and that community is power, big or small,” she began. “We need advocates, people who fight relentlessly for the care, the policies and the respect that moms deserve. And we need storytellers, people who show the real picture of this journey at every stage without judgment.”

That’s where Motherly can play a powerful role going forward, she noted.

“Motherly is growing from a trusted resource into an active community online and off,” she explained. “What does that mean in practice? It means we’re showing up in her group chat. We’re in her feed with a slate of new vertical video shows that I’m really excited about. We’re in her earbuds with a new podcast. And we’re popping up in her neighborhood with our new hyper local event series, coming to a neighborhood near you so that moms can find the people where they are.”

#7908. Fostering Is In My Blood

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

I remember when my mom brought home our first fosters. I was in fifth grade, and when my twin sister, Becca, and I came home from school, our mom walked us over to a box with three little neonatal kittens, just days old: Amelia, Angel, and Buddy. With closed eyes and little bodies running purely on instinct, they wriggled over one another, crying out to be fed. I watched as my mom gently picked them up, and as she did, she turned to us, smiling, and said, âtheyâre your responsibilityâ.

I was flooded with excitement and fear all at once. I knew nothing about caring for something so small. I watched in awe as my mom bottle-fed them one by one. The meowing subsided, and their little ears wiggled as they latched on and ate until their tiny bellies were full. The lesson had begun regardless of my fears. But feeding, I quickly learned, was just step one.

Soon after, we were stimulating each kitten to go potty, testing the temperature of their enclosure, wiping them clean, and getting them settled in for a post-bottle nap. So much happened so quickly, and they were so small and fragile. I told my mom I was nervous that I wouldnât be able to do what she did. She laughed and, with a grin, informed me I would have plenty of time to learn: Amelia, Angel, and Buddy would need to eat every 2 hours, even throughout the night. So we had lots of chances to practice and retain all the new skills she was showing us.

Over the next few weeks, we watched them grow and grow until they were ready to find their forever homes. As adoption day approached, it was incredibly hard. My sister and I begged our mom to let us keep the kittens. After all, we had raised them, and our love for them was undeniable. But she assured us that this was a good thing; letting them go meant we could help more animals in need. In the moment, however, I didnât understand. Instead, I cried myself to sleep holding the kittens. My kittens.

Then the day came, and even though the adopters were my friends, I bristled when they knocked at the door. But as they came in and met Amelia, Angel and Buddy, something magical happened: I watched my friends fall in love with them just like I had. They giggled at the clumsy way Buddy walked. Their hearts melted as they watched the girls cuddle in the sun. I was still scared to let the kittens go, but now part of me was excited, too. My friends saw them how I saw them. I had to trust that the little babies that we raised were on to bigger and better things. Things that would allow us to welcome another baby in need. But still, my heart broke - I had fallen in love with each of them, and saying goodbye terrified me.

There wasnât much time after they were adopted to worry about my fears, though. Before I knew it, we said hello to our next foster: a skittish and energetic 5-week-old boy we called Kipper. I thought maybe this time Iâd try to guard my heart, but Kipper stole it anyway. His silly antics and never-ending supply of energy made it impossible not to fall in love with him, too. Part of me hoped that maybe this time, Kipper could stay. But my mom held firm, and a few weeks later another friend came to us to adopt. I watched it play out all over again. I smiled as they swooned over this little precious kitten and all his quirks, just like I had.

This time, though I was still heartbroken, I felt a sense of understanding settle in, too. I remember thinking to myself, as Kipper fell asleep, purring, in my friendâs arms, âI wonder who we will get to help next?â

It didnât take long for that question to get its answer: Four tiny black-and-white kittens found in a hot tub and brought to our doorstep. Three were friendly; one, wellâ¦he was anything but! Cleo, Leo, and Brandy settled in beautifully, but Bindy just needed more.

More time, more attention, more understanding.

I felt drawn to him, and while my twin tended to the others, I found myself focused on Bindy. He would hide, hiss, spit, and bite. But really, he was just a little thing in a big world, and he was terrified. I worked with him every day, and slowly but surely, he made progress. When adoption day came around, however, we decided Bindy wasnât ready yet. He stayed behind to gain more confidence and, in time, became our first foster-fail.

Sometimes it was best for a foster to be adopted, but sometimes, they were already home.

Bindy eventually became the most loving cat I ever knew. He was my soul cat, and my best friend. And even though he stayed, I didnât avoid the heartbreak that came with saying goodbye; it just came many, many years later when old age finally took him. I learned a second lesson from Bindy then: there is no love without loss and, despite the pain, love would always be worth it.

So I continued to dive in, foster after foster. Heartbreak after heartbreak. Miracle after miracle. And it was always worth it; just like my mom said it would be. Iâm no longer the little girl learning from my mother; those lessons are now a part of me. Theyâre one of the things she left behind after a lifetime of love. My heart broke saying goodbye to her, too, but her teachings gave me a life thatâs filled to the brim with purpose. And paired with a passion inspired by my first foster fail, Bindy, I quickly developed a soft spot for the âspicyâ foster cats; and thatâs what I do now.

Currently, a euthanasia-list survivor is calling my home their safe haven. Just like Bindy, Simon wasterrified and aggressive, and he almost paid for it with his life. While Iâve been fostering him, however, Iâve gotten to know a completely different cat than the one in the shelter. A cat thatâs full of love and silly antics, whoâs eager to hold a conversation and meow for your attention. A cat who just needed a chance.

When his adoption day comes, I know my heart will break again; it always does. Itâs the price we pay for loving something, and Iâll pay that price over and over again because it means I get to watch someone adore him in all the ways I have, and more. The internet will go into an uproar demanding I keep him, but my momâs voice will sound clearly in my ear and keep me grounded:

âItâs a good thing. Letting them go means we can help others in need.â

So I'll say goodbye, knowing another Simon, Bindy, or Kipper is waiting for their chance to be loved. And as I walk back into the shelter, the lesson I began learning all those years ago in fifth grade remains true: Fostering Saves Lives.

As a third-generation animal rescuer, Rachael Rae Robertson has truly never had a moment where her life didnât revolve around animals â and she wouldnât have it any other way. Her grandmother had a farm for retired racetrack horses and farm animals, her aunt worked in wildlife rehabilitation, and her mom focused on pets like bunnies, dogs, birds, and cats. Though all three of these inspirational women are no longer here with us, their lessons remain. Now, Rachael hopes to share the gifts they gave her and her twin sister, Becca, with the world. With over 450k followers on TikTok and 190k on Instagram, Rachael documents her foster animals and their journeys, shedding light on the beautiful ups and downs of fostering while sharing the lessons sheâs gathered from her family, far and wide. She hopes to inspire others to dip their toes into the world of rescue, too, whether itâs through fostering, volunteering, or activism. In her free time, she can be found in her happy place â aka with her tetrad of tabbies and senior pup!

Can switching diapers alone fix my baby’s eczema? No. A fragrance-free, hypoallergenic diaper helps, but routine matters as much or more: change every two to three hours, use barrier cream at every change, give daily diaper-free time, and clean gently. And since eczema is a chronic condition, your pediatrician should be part of the plan.

Why does my baby’s rash only show up near the diaper elastic or leg cuffs? That pattern suggests a contact allergy to dye or elastic material rather than just general dermatitis. Have your pediatrician take a look.

#7906. 70+ Dogs Rescued From South Korean Meat Farm as 2027 Ban Approaches

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Nearly 30 dogs have arrived in New York after being rescued from a dog-meat farm in South Korea. Their journey toward adoption is beginning, but with the country's ban still months away from taking full effect, the work is far from over.

A plane ride to New York probably wasn't on these dogs' bingo cards. Neither, for that matter, was a soft bed, a full bowl of food, or the chance to be someone's beloved family member. After spending their lives confined to cages, even the simplest things may seem exciting and new.

On October 1, nearly 30 dogs were rescued from a dog-meat farm in Gangjin, South Korea, that once bred and slaughtered as many as 1,000 dogs each year. This was part of a larger rescue operation by Humane World for Animals that saved more than 70 dogs from the property.

For the organization, the operation marks its final large-scale dog-meat-farm rescue in South Korea ahead of the country's ban, which takes full effect on February 7, 2027. Humane World for Animals has rescued nearly 3,000 dogs from farms since 2015, making this a significant milestone.

And yes, it's a reason to celebrate. But before we get too comfortable patting ourselves on the back, there's a much bigger picture to consider. Getting these dogs out was a huge victory, but there are still thousands at risk.

When the rescue team arrived at the farm in Gangjin, in South Korea's South Jeolla Province, they were met with disturbing scenes. Rows of rusting cages, abandoned collars scattered on the ground, and skeletal remains served as a gruesome reminder of the dogs that hadn't been so lucky.

It's a hard reality to come to terms with, especially if your own dog is currently hogging the sofa, demanding snacks, or staring at you as though you've ruined their life by being five minutes late with dinner. The minor dramas faced by our beloved pets are a world away from what these poor dogs endured.

Humane World for Animals has reported finding mixed breeds and dogs of different sizes during its rescue work. The survivors included Jindos, a breed native to South Korea, a husky mix, and smaller dogs, including a spitz mix. In other words, any dog could end up on the menu.

In this most recent rescue, a concerned citizen alerted a local animal protection group, which contacted Humane World for Animals and the authorities. Officials found that the farm had broken South Korea's Animal Protection Act. The farmer, a man in his 80s, agreed to hand over the dogs and promised not to take part in the dog-meat trade again.

More than 70 dogs were rescued. Nearly 30 travelled to New York, another 12 went to a rehabilitation center in Montreal, and some mothers and their puppies remained in South Korea because they were too young to fly safely.

Rescuing dogs from situations like this isn't as simple as just opening a cage and booking the next available flight. International transport requires veterinary checks, vaccinations, documentation, and careful consideration about which animals are fit to travel. The priority is getting them out safely, not rushing them onto a plane for the sake of a happy headline.

South Korea passed its Special Act on the Termination of Breeding, Slaughter, and Distribution of Dogs for Consumption in January 2024. Its key prohibitions will finally take full effect on February 7, 2027, making it illegal to breed, slaughter, or sell dogs or dog meat for human consumption. But the transition is already underway.

In May 2026, South Korea's Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs reported that about 82% of the country's 1,537 registered dog-meat farms had closed. Over a thousand farms closed is something worth celebrating, but it means 272 farms are still operating.

Another consideration is that closing a farm doesn't automatically save the dogs living there. A business can shut down, the gates can close, and the paperwork can be signed, but where do all those dogs go?

According to Humane World for Animals, government figures indicate that of approximately 393,857 dogs counted on farms that had been closed, only 1,121 were adopted or transferred to public shelters. That's about 0.3%.

Itâs understood that most of these dogs were sent for slaughter or moved to other farms. So, while the closure of dog meat farms is good news, itâs not a true victory if these dogs are simply moved on to face the same fate. The ban is a huge step forward, but a law is only as good as its enforcement.

The real goal isn't just to close the farms. It's making sure the dogs are actually safe.

Getting out of the farm is the first big hurdle for these dogs. Now comes veterinary care, recovery, and the not-so-small task of learning how to live in a completely different world.

Humane World for Animalsâ rescue protocols include veterinary exams, vaccinations, respiratory screening when needed, and the health documents required for international travel. Each dog has their own needs. Some may need treatment for skin problems, wounds, dental disease, or nutritional deficiencies.

The second, and perhaps most challenging, hurdle for these dogs is adapting to a whole new way of life. Just because a dog has been saved doesn't automatically mean a dog feels safe.

Imagine never having lived in a home, then suddenly finding yourself surrounded by doors, stairs, strange noises, slippery floors, and humans who keep trying to show you how much they love you. Even a well-meaning hug could be overwhelming. And the vacuum cleaner? Let's just say it probably won't be winning any popularity contests.

These dogs may need to learn things many pets take for granted: how to explore a room, relax around people, or understand that a hand reaching toward them isn't something to fear. Some will be curious from the start. Others may prefer to watch from a safe distance. Neither response is wrong, and patience plus a little common sense go a long way.

A quiet place to rest, a predictable routine, and the freedom to explore without being pushed can help a dog settle in. Rewarding small steps with positive reinforcement builds confidence without turning every new experience into a test.

Adjusting to a new life takes time, and there's no need to rush it. A dog who hides under the table on day one isn't a failed adoption. A dog who isn't ready for cuddles isn't being ungrateful. Theyâre figuring things out, and they need time to decide that this strange new place might actually be safe. Building trust and confidence can be a slow process.

Those familiar with the process of adopting or fostering dogs, particularly those who may not have had the best start to life, may have heard of the 3-3-3 Rule for Dogs: 3 days, 3 weeks, 3 months. Itâs a simplified interpretation of the timeline many dogs tend to follow when adjusting to a new home environment.

The first 3 days are about decompression and resetting the nervous system. It might look like a dog that is timid, constantly moving, hiding, or even showing signs of aggression. Some dogs adjust quickly, while others may take a little longer than 3 days. The important thing to know is that this version of the dog is not usually a good representation of their true selves.

Over the first 3 weeks, dogs will start to gain confidence and explore their new world. They are often testing boundaries, becoming familiar with patterns, and learning how to trust. Being consistent and providing predictable routines is paramount to this process.

By the time 3 months have passed, most dogs will be feeling more settled. It may still take some time for their full personality to appear, but with every passing month, they become more confident, more trusting, and less anxious.

Sometimes progress looks like taking a treat from someone's hand. Sometimes it's finally falling asleep without startling at every sound. Those moments might not make a flashy before-and-after video, but for that dog, they're a big deal.

One more thing: fear and behavioural changes shouldn't automatically be dismissed as consequences of a dog's past. Pain, illness, and other medical problems can affect behaviour, too. If a dog seems persistently distressed or suddenly starts acting differently, a veterinary check is important. We don't want to assume it's trauma when there may be pain due to a treatable medical issue behind it.

A second chance isn't just getting a dog out of a cage. It's giving them the medical care, space, and time to discover that life can be safe, and maybe even pretty wonderful.

Humane World for Animals calls the Gangjin operation its final large-scale dog-meat-farm rescue in South Korea. But that doesn't mean the work is over. The organization plans to continue monitoring the ban and supporting efforts to enforce it.

Closing farms is a huge win. Full stop. But making sure dogs aren't left behind, moved elsewhere, or subjected to illegal practices is part of making that win count. With the ban taking full effect in February 2027, the coming months will be crucial.

For the dogs already rescued, a new life is finally within reach. Veterinary care. Rehabilitation. A chance to find a home where the biggest worry is whether they get the good spot on the sofa. That's quite the upgrade.

Now, we turn our attention to the dogs still waiting in South Koreaâs remaining farms. Stopping the dog meat trade is a huge victory, but in many ways, itâs just the beginning. Saving these dogs is more than just stopping the slaughter. Itâs making sure they all get the happy ending they deserve.

#7905. The Best Diapers For Diaper Rash, Ranked (2026)

If your baby’s bottom looks like a tomato by 3 p.m., the diaper matters as much as the cream.

If you’ve changed what feels like 400 diapers today, used enough cream to frost a sheet cake, and the rash is still winning, you’re not doing anything wrong. The good news is that rash-prone skin is super common, and it’s manageable. But (or butt, if you will) diaper rash prevention isn’t just about cream and wipes. The diaper matters too, and the best diapers for diaper rash handle moisture and let skin breathe. Turns out you don’t have to choose.

The one with actual clinical data behind it.

Pampers also says Swaddlers also have Dual Leak-Guard Barriers, are hypoallergenic, and have been fragrance-free in every size since June 2026.

When newborn sizes still look like a parachute.

For when you’re too tired to do the squish test.

Why: Huggies says these have a wetness indicator and are hypoallergenic and free of fragrance, parabens, and elemental chlorine.

Should I get a more absorbent or a more breathable diaper to prevent rash?

Both. Absorbency keeps wetness off skin, and breathability lets heat and humidity escape. Look for a diaper that does both.

Is a fragrance-free or an extra-absorbent diaper better for preventing diaper rash?

You want both in one diaper. Fragrance-free cuts down on irritants, while absorbency handles the moisture behind a lot of rash.

Is it worth paying more for a rash-preventing diaper, and which one is best?

Not necessarily. Frequent changes and barrier cream often matter more than price. Pampers Swaddlers is our top pick, backed by a Pampers-sponsored study showing 50% fewer instances of severe redness, at a mainstream price.

What’s the best rash-preventing diaper for a preemie with delicate skin?

Preemie skin needs extra-gentle materials, frequent changes, and clinician guidance before you switch products. Pampers says its Swaddlers Preemie diapers were developed with NICU nurses, are fragrance-free and hypoallergenic, and come in sizes P3 to P1 for babies under about 6 pounds.

Is a wetness-indicator diaper or an extra-absorbent diaper better for preventing rash?

Absorbency is what actually helps prevent rash. A wetness indicator is just a helpful reminder that it’s time to change.

Cats have only been domesticated for about half as long as dogs have. On top of that, their genes are much less susceptible to âshapingâ than those of dogs. The result? Cats have retained more wild feline physical traits, instincts, and tendencies than dogs.

Not only does this have a significant impact on feline behavior, but it also shapes how we care for them.

Cats are complex creatures, and it takes more than love, cuddles, and the occasional tasty treat to keep them truly engaged, enriched, and thriving. In fact, they often need more than what the average owner can provide with their own two hands.

I could go on all day about the importance of a high-quality diet for your cat. But today, I want to talk about an aspect of the feline diet most owners might not think about: the importance of small, consistent, proportioned meals.

Cats evolved as hunters of relatively small prey, so their natural feeding pattern is quite different from ours and from the typical pet dog.

A wild cat might spend much of its day moving through its territory, hunting, and eating multiple small meals when the opportunity presents itself. They are not accustomed to sitting down to one or two large meals each day.

Although the process of domestication means that your feline family member no longer needs to hunt down their next meal, those instincts haven't completely disappeared just because their food comes in a bowl.

Even more so than eating habits, drinking habits in cats are highly tied to their instincts and physiological needs.

Domestic cats evolved from desert wild cats. That arid climate impacted their relationship to water in two key ways:

First, desert wild cats evolved to get most of their water from their preyâwhich isnât much. This means their kidneys are highly specialized to retain water and pass very little of it through their urine. For a cat that eats several juicy mice each day, this is all well and good. For a pet cat eating dry food, the need to consume water is dramatically increased if they are to keep this super-efficient system running properly. However, the instinct to actively seek out drinking water has not entirely caught up with the domesticated catâs lifestyle.

This brings us to cat hydration key number two: Desert wild cats know better than to drink stagnant water. In hot, arid climates, still water breeds bacteria and other dangerous organisms. As a result, cats are naturally attracted to fresh, flowing water that is much safer to drink; something that remains true for our pets.

Your kitty may be a skilled hunter and the apex predator of your home, but, like their wildcat ancestors, they can also be prey animals, with instincts that evolved to evade larger predators. One place this becomes evident is in their bathroom habits.

Cats bury their urine and feces to hide the scent from potential predators and competitors, so a stinky litter box feels anything but safe. And if they donât feel safe there, they may find other places to eliminate waste. Or worse, hold it in, causing kidney and digestive issues.

#7903. Are Dogs the Secret to a Happier, Healthier Childhood?

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Dogs have been a fixture of family life for thousands of years, and many people who grew up with one say they canât picture their childhood without them. Beyond the obvious benefits of companionship and fun, growing up with a dog has been shown to have positive effects on physical and emotional well-being; advantages that show up in how children handle friendships, feelings, and everyday challenges.

Of course, this doesnât mean that having a dog is right for everyone. Bringing a dog into your home is a big decision that affects budgets and daily routines for years to come, and the best outcomes tend to come from families who go in with open eyes.

For anyone considering life with a dog, here are a few ways they can improve a childâs life, and things to consider before adopting one.

Growing up around animals can lower the chance of developing allergies later on. Dogs, and all the things that come with living with them, expose children to a range of allergens, which helps build a more robust immune system. The key seems to be early exposure, which means the sooner a dog becomes part of a childâs world, the better.

Children who are close to their dogs tend to be more securely attached to their parents, and theyâre more likely to form strong friendships, too. Strong relationships in one part of a childâs life seem to go hand in hand with strong relationships in others. Kids who share more physical contact with their dogs, from cuddles to roughhousing, tend to get along better with their moms, dads, and friends.

Kids who grow up with a family dog tend to have lower rates of anxiety. The benefits reach well beyond childhood, too. Dogs can ease feelings of depression and anxiety in adults who went through childhood trauma, and they can reduce signs of post-traumatic stress, which is part of the reason theyâre so often brought into therapy.

A dog is a living, breathing creature with needs, and children who help care for one learn responsibility and dependability. A five-year-old canât take on every chore, but age-appropriate tasks are a great place to start. Young children spend much of their lives at the mercy of parents and teachers, so having a dog to look after can give them a real sense of empowerment and build self-esteem.

Caring for an animal from an early age also builds empathy, which supports emotional intelligence and helps a child grow into a more compassionate person. The lessons go on from there. Dogs model loyalty; training and bonding teach patience, and learning to read a dogâs body language and respect their boundaries teaches respect. When a family pet eventually passes away, children also learn about death and grieving.

Children with pets tend to have better self-esteem than children without them. The effect appears to be strongest as kids approach adolescence; an age when the emotional support of a companion animal may matter most.

Families with dogs tend to be more physically active than their peers, getting about 11 extra minutes of exercise a day. That may not sound like much, but it adds up to roughly 5.5 hours a month in a society that is growing more sedentary all the time.

For some children, the effect is far larger. Girls in particular gained around 52 minutes of light physical activity a day after a dog joined the family. The flip side was striking too, since girls who lost their pet saw their daily activity drop by 62 minutes.

Children tend to handle stressful moments better with a dog nearby. They feel happier and more at ease, and being able to touch the dog calms them even further. Simply having a furry companion close by seems to help kids feel steadier inside.

For all the upsides, adopting a dog isnât a decision to take lightly, and there are a few things every family needs to consider before racing out to get a four-legged friend.

Budget: Dogs depend on their owners for food, veterinary care, and emergencies, and a household budget that canât cover those costs is a reason to rethink the plan.

Age: Although many childhood benefits increase the earlier they start living with a dog, sometimes waiting until children are older is a good idea. St. Bernards make fantastic family pets, for example, but they can weigh as much as 180 pounds and can hurt a child accidentally. Small breeds have their own risks, since they can be fragile and prone to injury until kids learn boundaries and how to respect animals.

Lifestyle: A family that works long hours and spends every evening shuttling children to activities needs a plan for what the dog will be doing. Not every schedule has room for a pet, and that is perfectly fine, but a dog shouldnât be adopted without free time to spend with it.

Motivation: Children often beg for a dog, promising to walk, feed, and pick up after them.

Then, the novelty fades, and the adults end up with the bulk of the care. Although itâs a good idea to encourage children to take on some of the responsibility of looking after a dog, you should assume that youâll be the one doing most of the work â hope for the best, plan for the worst!

Growing up alongside a dog can bring real benefits, from fewer allergies and lower anxiety to stronger relationships and more time spent moving. But to enjoy the benefits of living with a dog, families need to have the time, money, and genuine desire to take care of one.

Growing up with a dog might not guarantee health and happiness, but itâs a pretty good place to start!

#7902. School meals decoded: What’s really on the lunch tray

The menu in your child’s cafeteria isn’t set by chance. It’s the result of a multi-year federal process, and you can weigh in on how it changes.

By Lauren Ramakrishna Updated Nov. 23, 2026

This article is sponsored by Center for Science in the Public Interest (CSPI). Thank you for supporting the brands that support Motherly and mamas.

In my son’s school district, entering middle school is a rite of passage. Sixth graders go to a new building, get their own locker, and experience freedoms they weren’t allowed in elementary school.

When my son came home from his first day of middle school, I couldn’t wait to talk about it. “What was the best part of your day?” I eagerly asked. “The food,” he replied.

I wasn’t surprised. Meals are a big deal for a growing boy. But it did make me wonder, what exactly will he eat for lunch every day?

Long gone are the days when I would pack my son a homemade lunch with a loving note tucked inside. In middle school, he wanted to walk into the cafeteria, review the day’s menu options, stand in line, and buy his lunch. I agreed to the plan because I wanted to support his thirst for independence. But I also hoped I hadn’t unwittingly given him permission to start a junk-food-only diet.

Luckily, there are guidelines schools are required to follow when it comes to serving our kids meals. Those rules aim to make lunchtime enjoyable and healthy for the 30 million students who eat school lunch every day in the United States through the National School Lunch Program (NSLP). Unsurprisingly, they’re a constant work in progress.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) sets federal requirements for school meals served through the NSLP and the School Breakfast Program. The rules attempt to align school food offerings with nutrition standards outlined in the Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGA), the official dietary guidance published by the USDA and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) every five years. When the DGA gets an update, school nutrition standard changes will follow, as required by law.

Schools are currently implementing changes developed following the release of the 2020-2025 DGA. In April 2024, the Food and Nutrition Administration (FNA, formerly Food and Nutrition Service) , a government agency responsible for administering domestic nutrition programs, like the NSLP, issued a rule requiring schools to make changes to foods served at school, including:

These updates join a comprehensive list of nutrition standards for school breakfasts and lunches that outline weekly serving requirements for fruits, vegetables, grains, meats and meat alternatives, and milk, as well as calorie minimums and maximums, and limits on saturated fat.

The USDA and HHS released the 2025-2030 DGA on January 7, 2026, triggering the next wave of school nutrition reviews in preparation for new recommendations and requirements. The USDA will compare the new DGA guidelines against existing school nutrition requirements, then draft a proposed rule on which schools, state agencies, advocates, industry experts, and consumer advocacy groups, like Center for the Science in the Public Interest, can provide feedback. The USDA will read and respond to comments, sometimes changing planned provisions in response to the feedback received, then publish its final rule.

At face value, this may seem like a good thing.

The USDA and HHS appoints a Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee (DGAC) every five years to serve as an independent, expert panel of scientists and researchers in nutrition, health and medicine. The committee spends years reviewing current nutrition science to write a scientific report that’s typically used as a foundational resource for new dietary guidelines. DGAs have historically followed the vast majority of the DGAC’s recommendations. But, as CSPI notes, USDA and HHS rejected more than half of the DGAC’s expert recommendations. Instead, the agencies, according to CSPI,  “hand-picked authors whose work aligned with beef, dairy, and protein supplement industry interests and the administration’s preconceived policy goals.”

This group of hand-picked authors created a new “Scientific Foundation for Dietary Guidelines for Americans,” which includes contradictory advice, recommending folks stick to prior, science-based saturated fat limits, while suggesting high-fat foods like whole milk and beef tallow are part of a healthy diet.

CSPI has raised other concerns about the 2025-2030 DGA, arguing that it gives harmful guidance to emphasize animal protein; advises people to consume double or more of the scientifically-backed recommendation for daily protein; reduces clarity around how people can eat a balanced diet within vegetable and protein categories; and adopts an inverted food pyramid that doesn’t accurately visually represent the dietary recommendations found within the text of the guidelines.

As in cycles past, schools expect the USDA to use the most recent DGA as a guide to propose changes to school nutrition standards. It’s unclear exactly what changes will be put forth, but there will likely be a mix of nutrition wins and losses. It’s possible the new standards will reflect evidence-based nutrition guidance like increasing whole grains, protein, and whole fruit, and cutting back on added sugars, sodium, and refined grains in school meals.

However, it’s also likely the new proposed standards may stray from evidence-based guidance by calling for decreased vegetable variety and overall fiber intake due to a deprioritization of plant-based proteins and an overemphasis on high-fat foods like whole milk and beef (rather than a variety of protein sources).  For example, students could see more protein, like eggs and yogurt, at breakfast but miss out on a rainbow of vegetables and inclusive protein options like beans and tofu at lunch. Zooming out, meals lower in added sugars could be prioritized, while progress made on reducing saturated fat and sodium in school meals will be lost.

The best way to inform what your kids get on their breakfast and lunch trays at school is to make your voice heard. After proposing changes to nutrition standards, the government will open a public comment period where you can share your opinions about what should be included or excluded from school meals. When the proposed rule finally comes out, CSPI will make it easy to share your opinion through model comments and templates that will allow parents to comment directly on the proposed rule. Stay tuned for next steps by signing up for CSPI advocacy emails.

The regulatory red tape may seem overwhelming. That’s why non-profits like CSPI give parents tools to learn about school nutrition standards and enact change. To learn more about school nutrition standards, visit CSPI’s Healthier School Food advocacy page. If you’re ready to advocate for healthier school meals, check out CPSI’s Take Action page to get involved.

Snake plants tolerate a lot of neglect, but November is different. Shorter days, cold windows, and indoor heating all call for a change of routine.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most of the year, a snake plant really is about as hard to kill as people say. But that changes in November. The days get short, and the heat comes on, and the watering habit you kept all summer now leaves the potting mix wet for weeks. Yellow leaves and soft, mushy bases tend to follow.

Good snake plant care in winter is mostly about doing less and getting the timing right. Once light levels drop, your snake plant isn't growing much, so it uses far less water and needs no fertilizer at all. What it does need is a dry pot between drinks, steady room temperatures, and a spot out of the cold air that pools along windows.

Take a few minutes with your plant in front of you and work through five checks. Run through them now, then again on a gray afternoon in December. That alone considerably cuts the odds of losing a snake plant to winter.

Don't rely on a calendar when watering snake plants. A snake plant that needed water every two weeks in July might go a month or more between drinks in November. Its surface won't tell you much. So how do you know when it's dry? Push a finger down as far as it goes, or try the chopstick trick: push a wooden skewer to the bottom of the pot and pull it out. Damp mix clings to the wood and darkens it; dry mix leaves it clean.

If you're struggling to know when to water, then use a moisture meter for an accurate assessment, like the Xlux instant read probe, available from Amazon. Water only when the whole depth comes up dry, then let the pot drain fully. Leaves that go soft or flop over at the soil line usually mean the roots have sat wet too long.

Low light is something a snake plant tolerates, not something it grows well in. In November, the sun sits lower and the days are short, so a dim corner that was fine in June may now get very little light. Growth slows, and the mix stays wet far longer because the plant is barely drawing water.

A spot within a few feet (about a meter) of an east or west window helps. Make the move gradual, though – a plant that goes straight from a dim hallway into hours of direct south sun can scorch.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Without a bright window, a grow light like the Sansi Pot-Clip-On Grow Light, positioned a foot or so (30 cm) above the leaves, fills the gap.

On a cold evening, hold the back of your hand near the window where your snake plant sits. Chilly on your skin means chilly on the leaves, too. Blame single-pane glass, the gap under an outside door, or a nearby heating vent. Any of them can swing the temperature more than a snake plant can take – even while the thermostat reads fine.

Ordinary room temperatures are what you're after, roughly 60–85°F (16–29°C). Trouble starts if the plant sits below about 50°F (10°C) for long stretches. Leaves pressed against cold glass can develop soft, water-soaked patches. So at night, pull the pot back a foot or two (30–60cm) from the window.

If you want to see what the plant goes through after dark, then use a high/low thermometer, like the TempPro digital indoor thermometer, which displays both high and low temperature and humidity levels.

Tip the pot and look underneath. Drainage holes get plugged with compacted mix, a stray pebble, or roots that have grown through. In a decorative cachepot, a snake plant can stand in an inch (2.5 cm) of old water without anyone noticing. Lift it out and check. If the mix is still wet a week or more after you watered, it may have broken down and is holding too much moisture.

Winter is a poor time to disturb roots, so repotting snake plants is normally a spring job. The exception is a pot that won't drain at all – or a mix that stays soggy no matter what. Then a careful repot now beats rotting roots in March. For a replacement, choose a pot with a drainage hole and its own saucer, like this Vigoro ceramic planter from Home Depot. Fill it with a gritty potting mix, like Miracle-Gro Cactus, Palm, and Citrus Mix, which drains much faster than regular potting soil.

Look each leaf over, down to the soil line, for signs of common snake plant problems. If yellow is creeping up from the base and the leaf feels soft or mushy there, you're looking at overwatering and rotting roots. Cold damage can look a lot like it, though. Wrinkled or curling leaves usually mean the reverse: the plant went too long between drinks.

Next, check the crevices where leaves overlap for pests. Cottony white tufts there are mealybugs (Planococcus citri), and small tan or brown bumps that stay put when nudged are scale (Coccus hesperidum).

Dab a few with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol, then follow up with a ready-to-use insecticidal soap, like Garden Safe insecticidal soap, sprayed right onto the insects. It's far easier to deal with a dozen now than hundreds in February.

Put the fertilizer away until spring. A plant that isn't actively growing can't use the feed, so unused salts build up in the mix and can burn roots. Hold off on routine repotting for the same reason. Fresh mix and a bigger pot push a plant toward new growth right when the light to support it is lowest. Disturbed roots also recover slowly in a cool room.

Don't water your snake plant on a schedule just because the heat is drying out the air. Dry air and dry soil aren't the same thing, and a snake plant copes with dry air far better than it does with wet roots. For the next few months, you want it holding steady, not growing.

Run the same five checks again around the new year. In winter, a snake plant mostly needs the right spot and to be left alone. Give it that, and the one looking a bit tired in November is usually putting up new leaves by late spring.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#7899. Her friend died after giving birth. Now she’s writing legislation to save other moms

Home / Health & Wellness / Women's Health

By Cassie Shortsleeve Updated Nov. 24, 2026

Mothering America is a regular column from Motherly and Chamber of Mothers sharing moms’ stories from across the country, showing the power of coming together to make change. Each piece is part of a larger effort to ensure every mother and family in the U.S. has the support and care to be well.

In 2008, Lauren Underwood was in graduate school at Johns Hopkins, earning a master’s in public health, when she met a woman with a big, bright smile named Shalon Irving.

She never would have imagined the impact that friendship would have on her life’s work. Underwood would eventually become a U.S. representative for the state of Illinois, fighting to protect moms like Irving, who died before she could see her friend take office.

At the time, Irving, who already had her PhD, was coming back to school for additional training in public health. “We were just like regular girlfriends, passing notes in class and everything,” Rep. Underwood says.

The two—Rep. Underwood, a registered nurse, and Irving, an epidemiologist—stayed in touch through the years. In January 2017, Rep. Underwood served as a senior advisor at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and Irving worked for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). She had also given birth to a beautiful baby girl named Soleil.

Three weeks later, though, Irving wasn’t feeling well. “She went to the doctor several times, explaining that something wasn’t right,” Rep. Underwood remembers. On January 28, Irving died of complications related to high blood pressure. She was 36.

“Shalon had a career focused on ending health disparities, and she was so excited to become a mom,” Rep. Underwood says.

Today, Rep. Underwood is the architect of a series of 14 bills called the Momnibus, which was reintroduced to Congress this spring. The Momnibus addresses “every clinical and non-clinical factor” leading to preventable maternal deaths and disparities in this country; it’s evidence-based, data-driven, and offers states, communities, providers, and nonprofits the resources to help save moms like Irving’s lives. For Rep. Underwood, the Momnibus is personal.

While a member of Congress, Rep. Underwood is also a woman and a friend who, like too many in this country, lost a dear friend and felt a fire to make change.

Rep. Underwood recalls Irving’s funeral as devastating—particularly because many of those in attendance held positions of the highest authority in public health in this country. She remembers the head of the CDC speaking at Irving’s funeral and expressing bewilderment at her death.

For Rep. Underwood, it was no mystery why mothers like Irving die in childbirth and shortly thereafter. As a clinician, she had seen firsthand health disparities in action; as a Black woman, maternal mortality was an unfortunate “phenomenon where it’s just so common when you talk about the maternal crisis.”

Today, we know about 84 percent of pregnancy-related deaths like Irving’s are preventable—meaning that most of the moms who aren’t here today should be here, and could be here, with the proper supports in place. Black moms are more than three times as likely to die in pregnancy or the postpartum months than white women—a disparity that persists across income and education levels.

“People think higher education or higher income is protective. They think that if you are a healthcare worker, you’re going to get the best healthcare. If you know the risks, are self-aware, confident, and have agency, and you can speak up for yourself, then these kinds of things won’t happen to you. Shalon and her death fly in the face of all of those assumptions, and it breaks your heart.”

When she made the decision to run for Congress, Rep. Underwood knew that if she won, maternal mortality would be an issue she’d work on.

In 2018, Rep. Underwood became the youngest Black woman ever elected to Congress. She teamed up with Rep. Alma Adams (D-NC), who also had personal experience with maternal health: Adams’ daughter had experienced a very challenging labor and delivery, known in medical terms as severe maternal morbidity, or an experience that has lasting impacts on a mother’s health.

Together, in April 2019, the two formed the Black Maternal Health Caucus. At a crowded press conference, Rep. Underwood fought back tears. “To be in this moment with the dome of the Capitol behind us and these cameras and people asking questions and it’s this diverse, multi-generational, multi-ethnic, male and female moment of speaking about an issue that was so personal to me—I was just overcome,” she says. “It was a moment of power and resolve. It was an invitation. We were planting a flag, saying, ‘We’re here. We’re going to do this work. We know that there’s an opportunity to bring change.’”

Rep. Underwood didn’t expect the Black Maternal Health Caucus to grow into one of the largest bipartisan caucuses on the Hill. “We left that press conference and our phones started ringing, and it never stopped.”

Rep. Underwood has dedicated her career to ensuring everyone—moms included—has equitable healthcare so we can all feel our best. She’s also dedicated her career to ending the maternal mortality crisis. “We know exactly what to do. We just need to invest, have the resolve, and to say, ‘This is unacceptable. Let’s fix this issue.’”

She also reminds us that Congress works on the issues that members raise. “If a Member comes in and says, ‘This is important to my community, and this is an essential issue that we tackle,’ that’s how solutions advance.” Many of her ideas for bills, she says, come from your stories.

“Often, people think that their story doesn’t matter, and when they come in to advocate, they think they need to have statistics or be a walking encyclopedia,” Rep. Underwood says. “But we are in a relationship business, and connection is currency. The fastest way to build a connection is to share your humanity, tell your story, and invite space for that vulnerability.”

What that means for you: If you have a story to share, Members of Congress are home in their districts through the end of the month, with offices open Monday through Friday and available for meetings. (Not sure how to set up a meeting? Check out Chamber of Mothers’ ‘Moms at Recess’ guide, which includes step-by-step plans and tips for hosting a meeting with Members of Congress.)

Rep. Underwood also underscores the importance of being loud about solutions and progress in maternal health. She highlights the power of doulas, lactation consultants, and community support in maternal health—and the fact that, to date, one of the Momnibus’ 14 bills has been signed into law. Others have passed the House. The Momnibus has also unlocked more than $250 million for states, community organizations, researchers, and providers to save lives. (You can find out which projects are being funded with Momnibus dollars in your community through the Caucus’s Momnibus Money Tracker.)

“We want the news of a pregnancy to be a time of joy and hope and eager anticipation and wonder,” Rep. Underwood says. “This can’t just be a conversation around problems. We want people to know that we’re working on this, that we have their backs, and about the opportunities, help, and the resources that are available.”

#7898. War Dogs of History: Sergeant Stubby and the Birth of the American War Dog Legend

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Long before the United States military established an official war dog program, one small stray taught the Army what a dog could do in combat. His name was Stubby, and by the time the First World War ended, he had become the most decorated dog in American military history.

Stubbyâs story began in the summer of 1917 at Yale Field in New Haven, Connecticut, where the 102nd Infantry Regiment of the 26th âYankeeâ Division was training before deployment to France. A short-tailed, brindle-colored dog of uncertain breeding, likely part Boston terrier and part American bull terrier, wandered into camp and was adopted by Private J. Robert Conroy. Soldiers were not permitted to keep pets, but Stubby won over the men, and eventually the officers, by learning to mimic military customs. He reportedly marched in step with the troops and raised a paw to his brow in a passable salute.

When the 102nd Infantry shipped out for France, the transport ships barred dogs. Conroy smuggled Stubby aboard the SS Minnesota hidden beneath his overcoat. Conroyâs commanding officer discovered Stubby during the crossing, but his salute reportedly charmed the officer into letting him stay.

Once in France, Stubbyâs role shifted from morale booster to something closer to that of a working soldier. He entered combat on February 5, 1918, at Chemin des Dames, enduring shelling for over a month, and went on to serve through 17 battles over 18 months on the Western Front.

After surviving a mustard gas attack, Stubby developed a heightened sensitivity to the smell of gas. Historians and contemporary newspaper accounts credit him with warning his regiment of subsequent gas attacks before the men could detect it themselves. This allowed soldiers time to don their masks. He was also credited with locating wounded soldiers in no manâs land and comforting them until stretcher bearers arrived.

Stubbyâs most famous exploit occurred when he discovered a German soldier mapping the layout of Allied trenches. According to accounts preserved by military historians, Stubby seized the man until American soldiers arrived to take him prisoner. For this act, Stubby was informally promoted to the rank of sergeant, making him, according to most accounts, the first dog to receive a rank in the United States Armed Forces. This was, of course, an honorary and unofficial designation rather than a formal commission, since the military does not commission dogs.

During the April 1918 German offensive on the town of Seicheprey, France, Stubby was wounded in the chest and leg by grenade shrapnel while accompanying the 102nd Infantry in combat. After recovering, he returned to visiting wounded soldiers in the hospital, walking the wards to lift the spirits of recovering men.

Stubby returned home a celebrity. He led parades, attended war bond rallies, and met three sitting or future presidents: Woodrow Wilson, Warren G. Harding, and Calvin Coolidge. General John J. Pershing personally honored him at a 1921 ceremony for the 102nd Infantry Regiment, presenting him with a gold medal from the Humane Education Society, an award that, while not an official military commendation, cemented his reputation as the greatest war dog of his era.

Conroy went on to attend Georgetown University Law Center, and Stubby went with him, becoming the unofficial mascot of the Georgetown Hoyas football team. At halftime, he would nudge a football around the field to the delight of the crowd.

Stubby died in 1929, reportedly in Conroyâs arms. His remains were preserved and are held today by the Smithsonianâs National Museum of American History, where he wears the medals and blanket he wore during his years of service. In 2018, an animated film called Sgt. Stubby: An American Hero introduced his story to a new generation. That same year, the descendants of Conroy dedicated a life-sized bronze statue of him at the Connecticut Trees of Honor Memorial in Middletown, Connecticut.

Stubby served nearly a quarter century before the United States Army established a formal War Dog Program in 1942. He had no training pipeline, no breeding program, and no structure to recognize what he did. He was, in the truest sense, an amateur who became indispensable through instinct, loyalty, and repeated exposure to danger alongside the men who fed and sheltered him. Later advocates of formal military working dog programs often cite his legacy as early proof of concept: a dogâs senses, courage, and bond with a handler could save human lives on a modern battlefield.

Every military working dog story, whether it unfolded in the trenches of World War I or on a patrol in Afghanistan, is also the story of a partnership. Learning that history is one of the simplest ways to honor the generations of dogs and handlers who served side by side. If these stories have moved you, there are meaningful ways to help carry them forward.

Support retired dogs. Not every military working dog can retire to a family couch. The Ddamien Project provides lifelong homes for retired military, contract, and law enforcement dogs whose medical or behavioral needs make typical adoption difficult.

Learn more. The Military Working Dog Heritage Museum, founded by former K9 handlers, is gathering the photographs, documents, and firsthand accounts of the dogs and people who served. Its newsletter, The Paw Print, shares many of these stories with the public.

Keep today's working dogs strong. Canine Advancement Group, led by veterinarian Dr. Brian Farr, advocates for treating working dogs as the athletes they are, offering evidence-based guidance on fitness, welfare, and handler education.

Follow the national tribute. The National Service Animals Monument, planned for Washington, DC, will honor service animals and their handlers across military, law enforcement, and assistance roles, including generations of military working dogs.

These dogs are part of our history. By preserving their stories, honoring their service, and caring for the dogs still serving and those who have come home, we help make sure their legacy endures.

If Sergeant Stubby proved what an untrained stray could do in the First World War, Chips proved what a dog could do once the United States built an actual program around him. Chips became the most decorated American dog of World War II. His story also marks the moment the Army decided it should never again give such awards to an animal.
